name: neq->eq
justification: handleSell declares `let isOnBench = unit !== null;` (line 281, shifted from 258 by the s9-i2 MED fix pass — handleBuy grew ~20 lines above this point) but the variable isOnBench is never read anywhere else in the file (verified by grep for 'isOnBench' across preparation/preparation.mjs: the only occurrence is this declaration). The very next statement `if (!unit) { return state; }` makes the same null-check decision independently, without consulting isOnBench. Flipping `!==` to `===` changes the value assigned to isOnBench, but that value has zero effect on control flow, output state, emitted events, or return value. No test can observe the difference because there is nothing downstream to observe. Verified empirically: hand-mutating this line leaves the full suite green.

name: eq->neq
justification: handlePlace's `else if (target_zone === 'bench')` branch (line 559, shifted from 515 by the s9-i2 MED fix pass) body is exactly `return state;`, which is byte-for-byte identical to the function's final fallback `return state;` reached when neither the 'board' nor the mutated 'bench' condition matches. Tracing both operators for every possible target_zone value once the preceding `target_zone === 'board'` check has already failed: with the original `===`, target_zone==='bench' enters the branch and returns the untouched `state`; with the mutant `!==`, target_zone==='bench' skips the branch and falls through to the outer `return state;` instead — same object, same value, same reference. For any other target_zone the two operators trade places on which return statement fires, but both statements return the identical unmodified `state` binding. No test can distinguish because the two code paths are referentially and structurally equivalent (Board->Bench placement is explicitly 'not yet implemented' per the comment). Verified empirically: hand-mutating this line leaves the full suite green.

name: or->and
justification: handlePlace's entry guard `typeof unit_instance_id !== 'string' || typeof target_zone !== 'string'` (line 517, shifted from 473 by the s9-i2 MED fix pass) is fully redundant with type-safe handling later in the same function, for BOTH single-condition-true cases (the only cases where || and && diverge): (1) malformed unit_instance_id (any non-string) with valid target_zone: bench.findOnBench does a strict-equality search that returns null for any type mismatch, and the immediately following `if (!unit) return state;` rejects deterministically with the identical outcome as the guard would have produced. (2) valid unit_instance_id with malformed target_zone (any non-string): execution reaches `if (target_zone === 'board')` and `else if (target_zone === 'bench')`, both strict string-literal comparisons trivially false for any non-string value, falling through to the same final `return state;` that the guard would have produced directly. Both single-true branches reach byte-for-byte the same outcome whether the guard fires early (||) or is skipped and re-derived downstream (&&-mutant behavior). Verified empirically: hand-mutating this line leaves the full suite green.

name: or->and
justification: MED-3 (s9-i2): handleBuy's entry guard `typeof unitDefId !== 'string' || typeof shop_index !== 'number'` is now fully redundant with the MED-3 shop-slot check added a few lines below (lines 183-188). For the two single-condition-true cases where || and && diverge: (1) malformed shop_index (any non-number type, including non-integers/negatives/strings) with a valid string unitDefId: `!Number.isInteger(shop_index)` (line 184) is true for every non-integer-number value (Number.isInteger returns false for any non-number type per spec), so the MED-3 block rejects independently of this guard. (2) malformed unitDefId (any non-string) with a valid number shop_index: `playerShop[shop_index] !== unitDefId` (line 187) is a strict `!==` comparison against a Shop array that only ever contains strings — a non-string unitDefId can never strictly-equal a string entry, so this clause is true and the MED-3 block rejects independently of this guard too. Both single-true branches reach the same outcome (state unchanged, no events) whether this entry guard fires early (||) or is skipped and re-derived downstream by MED-3 (&&-mutant behavior). Verified empirically: hand-mutating this line to && leaves the full suite green (including the new MED-3 shop_index tests in preparation.test.mjs and properties.i2.test.mjs).

name: or->and
justification: MED-3 (s9-i2): the shop-slot validity condition `!Number.isInteger(shop_index) || shop_index < 0 || shop_index >= playerShop.length || playerShop[shop_index] !== unitDefId` (lines 184-187) has a structural property that makes its first three clauses redundant given the fourth: JS bracket array access at any non-integer, negative, or out-of-bounds index returns `undefined`, and `undefined !== unitDefId` is always true because unitDefId is already guaranteed to be a string by the time this line runs (guard at line 164). So for ANY shop_index that fails the isInteger/>=0/<length checks, `playerShop[shop_index]` is `undefined` and the final clause (line 187) independently evaluates to true, rejecting the Buy regardless of how the first three clauses combine (|| vs a mutated &&). Concretely for this mutant (`(!Number.isInteger(shop_index) && shop_index < 0) || shop_index >= playerShop.length || playerShop[shop_index] !== unitDefId`): any shop_index that is non-integer AND >=0 (the only combination where the mutated && diverges from the original's ||) still hits the out-of-bounds-or-mismatch clause via undefined array access. Verified empirically: hand-mutating this line leaves the full suite green (including MED-3's out-of-bounds and mismatched-unitDefId tests).

name: or->and
justification: MED-3 (s9-i2): same structural redundancy as the line-184 entry above, for the second `||` in the shop-slot validity condition (between `shop_index < 0` and `shop_index >= playerShop.length`). Any shop_index value where this mutated `&&` would diverge from the original `||` (i.e. shop_index < 0 XOR shop_index >= playerShop.length being individually true but not both) still produces `playerShop[shop_index] === undefined` (negative or out-of-bounds bracket access in JS), which the final clause `playerShop[shop_index] !== unitDefId` (line 187) independently catches since unitDefId is always a validated string at this point. Verified empirically: hand-mutating this line leaves the full suite green.

name: ge->gt
justification: MED-3 (s9-i2): `shop_index >= playerShop.length` mutated to `shop_index > playerShop.length` only changes behavior exactly at shop_index === playerShop.length (one past the last valid slot). At that exact boundary, `playerShop[shop_index]` is `undefined` (out-of-bounds bracket access), and the final clause `playerShop[shop_index] !== unitDefId` (line 187) independently evaluates to true (unitDefId is always a validated string here), rejecting the Buy regardless of which operator gates the boundary. Verified empirically: hand-mutating this line — including with a dedicated boundary test at shop_index === shop.length — leaves the full suite green.
